body: 1983 letter goodwill appendix: Blue Chip bought See's in 1972 for $25m when it had ~$8m net tangible assets and earned ~$2m after tax, i.e., ~25% on tangible assets 'with conservative accounting and no financial leverage.' 'Our first lesson: businesses logically are worth far more than net tangible assets when they can be expected to produce earnings on such assets considerably in excess of market rates of return. The capitalized value of this excess return is economic Goodwill.' Source of See's premium: 'a pervasive favorable reputation with consumers'; such a reputation 'allows the value of the product to the purchaser, rather than its production cost, to be the major determinant of selling price.' Other goodwill sources: unregulated government franchises (TV stations) and 'an enduring position as the low cost producer in an industry.' 1981 letter gives the inflation test - favoured businesses have '(1) an ability to increase prices rather easily (even when product demand is flat and capacity is not fully utilized) without fear of significant loss of either market share or unit volume, and (2) an ability to accommodate large dollar volume increases in business ... with only minor additional investment of capital.' Actionable for India (5-6% CPI): screen for pricing power proven in inflationary years (2010-13, 2022) - gross margin held while volume held - and low incremental capital per rupee of revenue growth. Brands, distribution moats and low-cost producers qualify; commodity converters usually don't.
title: Buffett 1983/1981: economic goodwill, consumer franchises and inflation-proof businesses (See's)

body: Computed by us from IIM Ahmedabad's Fama-French-Momentum data library (Dec-2025 release, survivorship-bias-adjusted monthly long-short factor returns; BSE+NSE stocks via CMIE Prowess DX; micro-caps below 10% of median market cap and sub-Rs1 stocks excluded; RF = 91-day T-bill). Jan-1994 to Dec-2025 (383 months): WML momentum CAGR +10.6% (arith 13.1%/yr, vol 24.5%, t=3.0), max drawdown -53% (Feb-Nov 2000), worst years 2000 -36%, 1998 -32%, 2009 -30% (momentum crashes at market rebounds). HML value CAGR +6.5% (vol 20.4%, t=2.3), max drawdown -59% (1994-2000), worst years 2018 -21%, 2019 -21%; best 2007 +49%, 2021 +39%, 2023 +35%; 2020-25 value CAGR +18.9% (the PSU/cyclical rerating). SMB size CAGR -3.8% (t=-0.85, not significant), max drawdown -86% (1995-2009), negative in 16 of 31 years - the 'small caps always win in India' story is not supported once micro-caps are excluded and the factor is measured long-short. Market factor (excess over T-bills) CAGR only +4.9% vs RF 6.9%, max drawdown -75% (1994-2001): Indian T-bills were a high hurdle. By decade, momentum was strongest 2015-25 (CAGR 12.8%, t=3.0, vol only 14.5%). Lessons: factor premia exist but come with multi-year droughts that test discipline; momentum and value are negatively timed (good diversifiers); size is a tilt, not an edge. Caveats: long-short paper portfolios before costs; data vary between releases.
title: IIMA factor library (1994-2025, computed): momentum and value paid in India; size did not - with 50-86% drawdowns
